title: The other cheek
hook: turn the other cheek; go the second mile (Matthew 5:38–41)
tomorrow: so which is it: let your light shine, or give in secret?

segments.voice: Six lines from this week: lift up mine eyes, wings of the morning, manifold works, every thing that hath breath, salt and light, and yesterday's, reconcile first. The sermon asked for peace. Today it asks for more.

Why carry a stranger's load twice as far? Start with a man who had to carry it the first time. On the day Jesus is led out to be crucified, Matthew says the soldiers found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name, and "him they compelled to bear his cross." A passerby, forced to carry someone else's load. Matthew never says what Simon felt about it. Hold that word: compelled.

Now the sermon. "Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." In between, a lawsuit: if someone takes your coat, let him have your cloak too. Then: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." Compel, the same English word the King James uses for Simon. Some readers hear the old law Jesus quotes as a limit on revenge, and the Talmud reads it as fair payment, not an injury for an injury. Notice the pattern: a slap, a coat, a mile, each one something taken. Jesus goes further: don't return the blow, and when you're forced to go one mile, choose a second. The first mile is taken from you. The second is yours to give. Christians have argued over how far this reaches. Peace churches like the Mennonites and Quakers read it as a call to refuse violence entirely; other Christians read it as a rule for personal insult, not a ban on protecting the weak. Both read the same verse. What they share is the turn: from what's done to you to what you freely add.

segments.voice: Stand up and walk a short loop of the room, or down the hall and back. Then go around once more, slower, as a gift instead of a chore. Sit when you're done and feel the difference between the two.
The other cheek: Jesus's answer to a blow, not returning it, and when forced to go one mile, going two.
Carry this one: the second mile, the one nobody can make you walk. A week of old lines, done.

howItsDone: Christians read Matthew 5:38–41 in different ways: peace churches such as the Mennonites and Quakers as a call to nonviolence, other churches as a rule for personal insult; 'going the second mile' is a common phrase for freely giving more than is asked.

fork.setup: your neighbor asks you, again, to sign for his package while he's at work. what would the second mile look like?
options: sign for it, and then carry it to his door when he gets home.
sign for it, but tell him firmly this is the last time.
say no; turning the other cheek doesn't mean being used.
fork.reveal: the first mile is the favor asked; the second is the one you add freely. not every request deserves a yes, but this one is small.

chat.meaning: Jesus says when you're compelled to go a mile, go twain. The first mile is asked or taken; the second is freely given.

tie.story: Jesus said, if someone compels you to go a mile, go two; Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry a cross.
tie.friend: Zoe's ride is the mile Theo asked for; the breakfast is the second mile she chooses.
